steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Sensing the flow of transparent media like air or water is important for many applications, from aerodynamics to gas leakage detection. Optical imaging is a useful tool to examine transparent media because it can capture them remotely with high detail in space-time. Among the existing methods, schlieren imaging is a simple but efficient optical tool to see the “invisible”: inhomogeneities in transparent media that are not necessarily perceived by the naked eyes. The recording settings it needs are simple: lenses, cameras, and mirrors or background patterns, to image how light rays deviate because of refractive index variations in the media. It was first conceived as a visualization technique, but recent developments in schlieren and shadowgraphy have extended its usage to velocimetry. However, to analyze the velocity of the flow, such as convection, a high-speed camera with a large spatial resolution is needed. This is a constraint for real-world applications and also a limitation of the methodology, because: (i) high shutter speeds need unnaturally bright illumination, which is not always practical, (ii) transmitting and processing the large amount of redundant data that is acquired involves high bandwidth, storage, and power-hungry components, and (iii) even with the large power consumption, the trade-off between speed and spatial resolution limits the accuracy of estimating the flow velocity.

Event cameras are novel bio-inspired sensors. They respond to pixel-wise intensity changes, which conventional frame-based cameras cannot always see. They have advantages such as high speed, high dynamic range (HDR), low power consumption, and data efficiency (temporal redundancy suppression), so they are potential candidates to overcome the limitations of traditional (i.e., frame-based) schlieren techniques. But even with these potential capabilities, applying event cameras to imaging applications is still to be explored and developed.

In this paper we present a novel technique, event-based background-oriented schlieren (BOS), for sensing air convection with event cameras, and we propose a novel method to estimate the temporal derivative of air density from events and frames (Fig. 1). In the paper we tackle these challenges of event-based BOS: (i) Theory. No mathematical theory is established for event-based schlieren techniques. (ii) Data. Event cameras only sense increments of schlieren, instead of the larger differences with respect to a reference in frame-based BOS. (iii) Methodology. The origin of events in BOS (flickering, because they only happen at the edges of the background pattern) and large amounts of noise are novel and difficult for previous work in event-based vision. (iv) Evaluation. It is not easy to obtain the real-world ground truth of the air density, so we need some proxy ground truth and baselines.

- Approach
  - theoretical connection schlieren <-> events; flickering events, more direct than frames; high speed, challenging lighting
  - extend linearized event generation model, physically-inspired parameterization -> temporal density fluctuation
  - evaluation through optical flow; co-located frame-based camera for benchmarking
  - results: (i) recovers flow vs. frame-based and baseline methods (ii) flickering events more direct (iii) poor lighting (iv) slow-motion schlieren analysis
- Contributions
  - novel method combining events and frames (Secs. III and IV), via linearized event generation model
  - first schlieren event-frames dataset (Sec. V), 1 Mpixel, synchronized and calibrated
  - thorough comparison with baselines (Sec. VI)
  - simulation experiment with high-speed frame data (Sec. VII)
- First work showing advantages of event cameras for schlieren

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Sensing the flow of transparent media like air or water is important for many applications, from aerodynamics to gas leakage detection. Optical imaging is a useful tool to examine transparent media because it can capture them remotely with high detail in space-time. Among the existing methods, schlieren imaging is a simple but efficient optical tool to see the “invisible”: inhomogeneities in transparent media that are not necessarily perceived by the naked eyes. The recording settings it needs are simple: lenses, cameras, and mirrors or background patterns, to image how light rays deviate because of refractive index variations in the media. It was first conceived as a visualization technique, but recent developments in schlieren and shadowgraphy have extended its usage to velocimetry. However, to analyze the velocity of the flow, such as convection, a high-speed camera with a large spatial resolution is needed. This is a constraint for real-world applications and also a limitation of the methodology, because: (i) high shutter speeds need unnaturally bright illumination, which is not always practical, (ii) transmitting and processing the large amount of redundant data that is acquired involves high bandwidth, storage, and power-hungry components, and (iii) even with the large power consumption, the trade-off between speed and spatial resolution limits the accuracy of estimating the flow velocity.

Event cameras are novel bio-inspired sensors. They respond to pixel-wise intensity changes, which conventional frame-based cameras cannot always see. They have advantages such as high speed, high dynamic range (HDR), low power consumption, and data efficiency (temporal redundancy suppression), so they are potential candidates to overcome the limitations of traditional (i.e., frame-based) schlieren techniques. But even with these potential capabilities, applying event cameras to imaging applications is still to be explored and developed.

In this paper we present a novel technique, event-based background-oriented schlieren (BOS), for sensing air convection with event cameras, and we propose a novel method to estimate the temporal derivative of air density from events and frames (Fig. 1). In the paper we tackle these challenges of event-based BOS: (i) Theory. No mathematical theory is established for event-based schlieren techniques. (ii) Data. Event cameras only sense increments of schlieren, instead of the larger differences with respect to a reference in frame-based BOS. (iii) Methodology. The origin of events in BOS (flickering, because they only happen at the edges of the background pattern) and large amounts of noise are novel and difficult for previous work in event-based vision. (iv) Evaluation. It is not easy to obtain the real-world ground truth of the air density, so we need some proxy ground truth and baselines.

First, we develop a theoretical connection between schlieren and events, which shows that event cameras can sense the inhomogeneities of transparent media more directly (as flickering events) than frame-based cameras. Sensing schlieren directly through event data lets us observe air convection at high speed more precisely and in challenging lighting conditions. Second, we propose a novel method that extends the linearized event generation model with a physically-inspired parameterization to estimate the temporal density fluctuation due to the schlieren. Third, to evaluate the estimated density change, whose real-world ground truth is not easy to obtain, we establish an evaluation method using optical flow, by revealing the theoretical connection between temporal density change and optical flow (i.e., pixel displacement). With a co-located frame-based camera we can benchmark different methods of estimating temporal density change as a computer vision problem. The experimental results show that: (i) our method recovers the flow that corresponds to the temporal change of density gradient, by comparing with the standard frame-based methods and other baseline methods, (ii) flickering-like events are a more direct measurement of schlieren, (iii) event cameras record the density inhomogeneities even in poor lighting conditions, which state-of-the-art frame-based algorithms cannot provide, and (iv) the high temporal resolution of event cameras allows slow-motion schlieren analysis.

The main technical contributions of this work are:

- A novel method that computes schlieren by combining events and frames (Secs. III and IV). The method is rigorously obtained and well connected with the physical model of the sensors involved through the linearized event generation model.

- The first schlieren event-frames dataset (Sec. V). We publicly provide recordings of several schlieren scenes with events and frames, at high resolution (1 Mpixel), accurately synchronized and calibrated with an in-house acquisition system.

- A thorough comparison with baseline methods, even though truly ground truth data is lacking for this type of turbulent fluid dynamics phenomena (Sec. VI).

- A simulation experiment based on the high-speed frame data from earlier work to confirm the results of event-based BOS with those from frame-based BOS (Sec. VII).

As far as we know, this is the first work that shows the potential advantages of event cameras for schlieren imaging applications.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Sensing the flow of transparent media, such as air or water, is important for various applications from aerodynamics to gas leakage detection. Optical imaging is a useful tool for examining such transparent media because it can capture them remotely with high detail in space-time. Among existing methods, schlieren imaging is a simple but efficient optical tool for seeing the “invisible” [1,2]: inhomogeneities in transparent media that are not necessarily perceived by the naked eyes. It requires simple recording settings: lenses, cameras, and mirrors or background patterns to image how light rays deviate due to refractive index variations in the media. While it was initially conceived as a visualization technique, recent developments in schlieren and shadowgraphy have extended its usage to velocimetry [2,3]. However, analyzing the velocity of the flow, such as convection, requires a high-speed camera with a large spatial resolution. This is not only a constraint for real-world applications but also a limitation of the methodology because: (i) achieving high shutter speeds requires unnaturally bright illumination, which is not always practical, (ii) transmitting and processing the large amount of redundant data acquired involves high bandwidth, storage, and power-hungry components, and (iii) despite the large power consumption, the trade-off between speed and spatial resolution limits the accuracy of flow velocity estimation.

Event cameras [4,5] are novel bio-inspired sensors that respond to pixel-wise intensity changes, which are not always visible to conventional frame-based cameras. They offer advantages such as high speed, high dynamic range (HDR), low power consumption, and data efficiency (temporal redundancy suppression) [6], which make them potential candidates for overcoming the limitations of traditional (i.e., frame-based) schlieren techniques. However, despite these potential capabilities, the application of event cameras to imaging applications remains to be explored and developed.

This paper presents a novel technique, event-based background-oriented schlieren (BOS), for sensing air convection with event cameras, and proposes a novel method to estimate the temporal derivative of air density from events and frames (Fig. 1). Throughout the paper, we tackle the following challenges of event-based BOS: (i) Theory. There is no established mathematical theory for event-based schlieren techniques. (ii) Data. Event cameras sense only increments of schlieren, as opposed to the larger differences with respect to a reference in frame-based BOS. (iii) Methodology. The origin of events in BOS (flickering, because they happen only at the edges of the background pattern) and large amounts of noise are novel and difficult for previous work in event-based vision. (iv) Evaluation. The real-world ground truth of the air density is not easy to obtain, so we need some proxy ground truth and baselines.

First, we develop a theoretical connection between schlieren and events, showing that event cameras can sense the inhomogeneities of transparent media more directly (as flickering events) than frame-based cameras. Such direct sensing of schlieren through event data enables us to observe air convection at high speed more precisely and under challenging lighting conditions. Second, we propose a novel method that extends the linearized event generation model with a physically-inspired parameterization to estimate the temporal density fluctuation due to the schlieren. Third, to evaluate the estimated density change, whose real-world ground truth is not easy to obtain, we establish an evaluation method using optical flow by revealing the theoretical connection between the temporal density change and optical flow (i.e., pixel displacement). A co-located frame-based camera enables us to benchmark different methods of estimating temporal density change as a computer vision problem. The experimental results show that: (i) our proposed method recovers the flow that corresponds to the temporal change of density gradient, by comparison with the standard frame-based methods and other baseline methods, (ii) flickering-like events are a more direct measurement of such schlieren, (iii) event cameras record the density inhomogeneities even in poor lighting conditions, which state-of-the-art frame-based algorithms cannot provide, and (iv) the high temporal resolution of event cameras enables slow-motion schlieren analysis.

The main technical contributions of this work are:

- • A novel method for computing schlieren by combining events and frames (Secs. III and IV). The proposed method is rigorously derived and well connected with the physical model of the sensors involved via the linearized event generation model.

- • The first schlieren event-frames dataset (Sec. V). We publicly provide recordings of several schlieren scenes by means of events and frames, at high resolution (1 Mpixel), accurately synchronized and calibrated using an in-house acquisition system.

- • A thorough comparison with baseline methods despite the lack of truly ground truth data for this type of turbulent fluid dynamics phenomena (Sec. VI).

- • A simulation experiment based on the high-speed frame data from [3] to confirm the results of event-based BOS against those from frame-based BOS (Sec. VII).

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to show the potential advantages of event cameras for schlieren imaging applications.
